newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE - Brazil govt crop estimate only due in 1997.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE - Brazil govt crop estimate only due in 1997.

text.p: A government estimate of Brazil's 1997/98 coffee crop is only expected in 1997, with the first - albeit preliminary - forecasts of the coming harvest likely to come from agriculture secretariats, federations and private consultants, officials said.

"The government is hoping to have an official estimate ready by March but until then it will use forecasts from regional bodies," said Luiz Moricochi, agronomist at Sao Paulo state Institute of Agricultural Economics (IEA).
"The government itself will not be making a forecast...What we intend to do is work with the states," said an official from the Industry and Commerce Ministry's National Coffee Department.
Devising a reliable and authoritative forecasting system is one of the goals of the recently-created coffee council which unites the public and private sectors.
However officials and agronomists are said to be still discussing the exact system and methodology to be used.
Meanwhile organisations such as the IEA and the Agricultural Federation of Minas Gerais State (FAEMG) are going ahead with their own regional and national surveys.

FAEMG next week is to begin a survey in which it will canvass producers who contributed to a state crop profile released earlier this year in which the state's 1996/97 harvest was forecast at 12.42 million 60-kg bags.
Results of the survey are likely to be ready at the beginning of December, a FAEMG official said.

Leon Yallouz, the former representative of the U.S. Department of Agriculture who was responsible for Brazil coffee estimates until earlier this year, will be producing his own forecast for private clients between November 20-30, he said.
Producers for some time have been predicting a smaller national harvest in 1997/98 and in some areas predictions, if anything, have become more pessimistic over the past month.
However it is still by no means clear what will be the overall pattern for Brazil, the IEA's Moricochi said.

"I have been speaking to many large farms who say they expect an increase in their production this year. A while ago I was expecting a drop, now however I could see the same crop as this year but it is still too early to say," he added.
In the Cerrado region of Minas Gerais state, the Coffee Co-operatives Center (Caceer) is most definitely expecting a drop, with a forecast of around 1.5 million bags against 3.2 million this year.

"The main reason is that we had a very high crop this year and the trees have to recover. In the area around Patrocinio for example the yield was around 33 bags per hectares compared with a four-year average of 18 bags," a Caceer official said.
"This was very high. Basically, the plants produced the size of two harvests in one year," he added.

In Varginha, coffee from the 1996/97 harvest is still arriving at the cooperative where producers are revising downward their original forecasts for this year's crop to 450,000 bags from expectations of 500,000 bags.
In addition rains at the beginning of September which helped flowerings for the coming harvest have on the other hand affected the quality of some beans.

"The rains mean that you have dark, ugly beans with a horrible taste which are difficult to sell for export or in the internal market," said Antonio Araujo da Silva, commercial director at the co-operative.
For 1997/98, production in the region could fall to around 270,000 bags, da Silva said.

In the north of Sao Paulo state, producers in the Franca cooperative have also revised downward their evaluation of the recent harvest to 450,000 bags from a hoped-for 500,000 bags, with some 20 percent affected by the late rains.
The main flowering for the 1997/98 crop took place in October and already expectations are of a harvest as low as 300,000 bags, the co-operative's agronomist said.

The most positive outlook however remains for the state of Parana where production was sharply hit by the 1994 frosts but where 1997/98 output is forecast to reach up to two million bags against one million to 1.2 million bags this year.
-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
